title: Height, Weight, and Body-Mass Index

unit.title: Clinical Office Practice and Patient Safety

sections.learningObjectives:
- Measure height and weight accurately using the correct equipment and technique.
- Explain BMI concepts, calculation, and standard adult and pediatric interpretation.
- Document measurements accurately and correct errors without falsifying the record.
- Protect patient privacy and dignity throughout measurement and communication.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Height is how tall someone is, measured from the floor to the top of their head. In the United States we usually write it in inches, like saying someone is 65 inches tall.

### Question 2

Weight is how heavy someone is. In the United States we usually write it in pounds, like saying a patient weighs 150 pounds.

### Question 3

A kilogram is a metric 'heavy unit,' and one kilogram is about 2.2 pounds. To change kilograms into pounds, you multiply by 2.2, like trading in bigger coins for more smaller coins.

### Question 4

BMI is short for 'body mass index.' It is a quick number doctors use to guess whether a person's weight is in a healthy range for their height.

### Question 5

BMI is a math problem that uses only two numbers: how heavy someone is (weight) and how tall they are (height).

### Question 6

Think of the healthy BMI range like a target zone on a game: a number from 18.5 to 24.9 is in the 'just right' zone for most adults.

### Question 7

BMI is like a warning light on a car dashboard. It does not fix anything by itself, but it tells the doctor to look more closely at whether weight might be a problem.

### Question 8

A stadiometer is a tall ruler attached to a wall with a sliding bar that rests on top of a person's head to show how tall they are.

### Question 9

A scale is like a bathroom scale at a doctor's office, but it is checked often to make sure it reads correctly.

### Question 10

Before using a scale, you make sure it says zero when nobody is on it, like resetting a kitchen scale before you pour in flour.

### Question 11

If you weigh yourself with heavy shoes on, the scale counts the shoes too. Taking them off means the number is just you.

### Question 12

If you stand on tiptoe or wear thick soles, you look taller than you really are. Taking shoes off lets the ruler measure your real height.

### Question 13

A BMI of 30 or more is in the highest category on the adult chart, called obesity.

### Question 14

A BMI under 18.5 is in the 'underweight' zone, which means weight is lower than the healthy range.

### Question 15

The 'overweight' zone sits between the healthy zone and the obesity zone, from 25.0 to 29.9.

### Question 16

Babies cannot stand on a ruler, so we lay them flat on a board and measure from the top of the head to the bottom of the feet.

### Question 17

The assistant is like a careful measurer who writes down the exact number and hands it to the doctor, who decides what it means.

### Question 18

If you write down the wrong height or weight, the doctor's math about a patient's health will be wrong too, so the real number matters a lot.

### Question 19

A person's weight is private, like a secret number. We measure it quietly in a private spot and do not announce it where others can hear.

### Question 20

The assistant can do the measuring and the math, but the doctor is the one who explains what the BMI number means for the patient's health.

### Question 21

BMI is a shortcut that guesses about body fat using height and weight, but it does not actually see how much fat a person has.

### Question 22

BMI is a division problem: take how many kilograms someone weighs and divide by their height in meters, squared.

### Question 23

You write the number in the patient's official chart right away, the same way you write homework answers in your notebook instead of trying to remember them.

### Question 24

To read a ruler correctly, you look straight at the mark, not from the side. The same is true for the height stick.

### Question 25

First square the height (1.75 x 1.75 = 3.0625), then divide the weight by that number: 70 divided by 3.0625 is about 22.9.

### Question 26

Square the height in inches, multiply the weight by 703, then divide: 703 times 150 is 105,450, and 105,450 divided by 4,225 is about 25.

### Question 27

To change pounds into kilograms, divide by 2.2. A 110-pound person is about 50 kilograms.

### Question 28

To change kilograms into pounds, multiply by 2.2. An 80-kilogram person weighs about 176 pounds.

### Question 29

A meter is 100 centimeters, so 170 centimeters is 1.70 meters, like 100 pennies make a dollar.

### Question 30

To measure height, the patient stands straight like a soldier against the wall with heels, back, and head touching, and looks straight ahead.

### Question 31

A tall hat or big hair bun adds inches that are not really the person's height, so we remove or flatten them before measuring.

### Question 32

Your weight changes a little during the day, like a water bottle that is fuller after lunch. Weighing at the same time each visit makes the numbers fair to compare.

### Question 33

Wearing heavy boots and a thick coat adds pounds that are not really you, like carrying a heavy backpack onto the scale.

### Question 34

Write down exactly what the scale says, like copying a number from a calculator instead of guessing a rounder number.

### Question 35

If you write the wrong number, draw one neat line through it, write the right number, and sign and date it, so everyone can see what was changed and why.

### Question 36

You should never write down a number you did not actually measure. That would be like writing an answer you did not really get on a test.

### Question 37

27.4 is between 25.0 and 29.9, so it lands in the 'overweight' zone.

### Question 38

BMI only knows total weight, not what the weight is made of. Muscle is heavy, so a strong athlete can score high on BMI even with very little fat.

### Question 39

As people age, they may lose muscle and even a little height, so the BMI number does not always mean the same thing it did when they were younger.

### Question 40

Kids are still growing, so doctors compare their BMI to other kids of the same age using a growth chart, like seeing how tall you are compared with classmates.

### Question 41

Your weight can go up or down a little each day depending on food and water, but your height stays pretty much the same day to day.

### Question 42

If someone cannot stand, we use a special scale their wheelchair can roll onto, or a safe lift, so we get a real weight without any risk of falling.

### Question 43

If a patient says no to the scale, we say okay, write down that they declined, and tell the nurse or doctor so they know.

### Question 44

A kind assistant just says the number without making any mean or judge-y comment, like reading a score without saying if it is good or bad.

### Question 45

We talk about 'a patient with a certain BMI,' not 'a fat patient.' We describe the measurement, not put a mean label on the person.

### Question 46

Getting weighed is a private moment, so it happens behind a closed door or curtain so nobody else watches or hears.

### Question 47

The assistant can say 'Your weight is 160 pounds today; the doctor will go over it with you,' instead of guessing whether it is healthy.

### Question 48

Stand like a statue in the middle of the scale with both feet flat so the scale gets a steady, correct number.

### Question 49

If the scale gives a surprising number, check the scale and weigh again, then tell the doctor so everyone is sure it is right.

### Question 50

You cannot solve a math problem before you have the numbers, so measure height and weight first, then do the BMI math.

### Question 51

Taller people weigh more just because they are bigger. Squaring the height helps make the comparison fair, like measuring cups per person rather than total cups.

### Question 52

Writing '154.3' without saying pounds or kilograms is like writing '50' without saying dollars or cents; nobody knows what you mean.

### Question 53

Every measurement gets a date and time stamp, like putting the date on your schoolwork so you know when you did it.

### Question 54

Different scales can be like two rulers that are slightly off. Using the same one each time keeps the numbers fair to compare.

### Question 55

A balance-beam scale is like a seesaw; you slide weights until it is perfectly level, then add up the numbers on both bars.

### Question 56

Wait for the digital numbers to stop changing, then read the steady number, like waiting for a countdown to finish.

### Question 57

A height ruler needs to be straight and tight, like making sure a measuring tape is not bent, or the numbers come out wrong.

### Question 58

If someone cannot stand straight, we measure as best we can and write a note about it, so the doctor knows the number may not be perfect.

### Question 59

If the number changed a lot, weigh again the same way and let the doctor know, instead of guessing whether it is a mistake or a real change.

### Question 60

Grown-ups use fixed BMI zones, but growing kids are compared to other kids their age using a growth chart, like percentile ranks in school.

### Question 61

If someone wore thick shoes last time or stood differently, the number can look different. We keep the setup the same so we can trust the numbers.

### Question 62

Keep every measurement with its date, like keeping a growth chart of your height over the years, so you can see the pattern.

### Question 63

Square 70 to get 4,900, multiply 200 by 703 to get 140,600, then divide: 140,600 divided by 4,900 is about 28.7.

### Question 64

There are 2.54 centimeters in an inch, so 64 inches is about 162.6 centimeters, which is 1.63 meters.

### Question 65

If the patient says one number and the scale says another, re-check the scale and weigh again, write down what the scale really says, and tell the doctor about the difference.

### Question 66

Square 1.60 to get 2.56, divide 64 by 2.56 to get 25.0, and 25.0 is the start of the 'overweight' zone.

### Question 67

A bodybuilder can be heavy with muscle and little fat, so their BMI number looks high even though their body fat is low. BMI is just a rough screen.

### Question 68

There are 12 inches in a foot, so 5 feet is 60 inches, and adding 7 more makes 67 inches.

### Question 69

Two people can have the same BMI number but look very different, one with muscle and one with fat, because BMI does not see inside the body.

### Question 70

If the scale shows both units, read the one you need and write it down with the right label, like choosing the right price tag in dollars.

### Question 71

Lying down to be measured usually gives a slightly longer number than standing up, so switching methods can make it look like the child shrank or shot up when they did not.

### Question 72

If the scale is wobbly or on a slippery floor, do not use it; tell someone so it can be fixed or moved to a safe spot first.

### Question 73

BMI is like a smoke detector: it beeps to say 'check this out,' but a doctor still has to look more closely to figure out what is really going on.

### Question 74

Since height gets squared in the BMI math, writing someone a little too short makes the BMI come out a little too high.

### Question 75

First change 150 cm to 1.50 m, square it to get 2.25, then divide 54 by 2.25 to get 24.

### Question 76

If someone feels nervous about the scale, be extra kind: weigh them in private and just say the number plainly with no mean comments.

### Question 77

The adult BMI chart uses the same number lines for everyone, even though men's and women's bodies can be built differently, which is one reason doctors look at more than BMI.

### Question 78

If a number in the chart looks impossible, like a 12-foot-tall person, do not use it; point it out so it can be fixed the right way.

### Question 79

As people get older, their spine can settle a little, so they may measure a bit shorter than before. That can be normal, not a mistake.

### Question 80

If someone is wearing a heavy cast, we still weigh them but write a note that says 'has a cast on,' so the doctor knows some of the weight is the cast.

### Question 81

One number is a snapshot, but several numbers over time tell a story, like watching your plant grow a little each week instead of checking it once.

### Question 82

Squaring means multiplying the number by itself: 1.8 times 1.8 is 3.24.

### Question 83

Make sure you are writing the number on the right person's paper, like putting your name on your own test so the grade goes to you.

### Question 84

A high BMI just means 'let's look closer,' especially for someone with a lot of muscle. The doctor checks more before saying anything for sure.

### Question 85

For kids, doctors use a special growth chart that compares the child's BMI to other children the same age, like a class ranking, instead of the adult number zones.
